user_input: Does my adult dog need a leptospirosis booster every year?
reference: An adult dog needs a leptospirosis booster once a year. The vaccine's protection lasts at least 12 months (some manufacturers guarantee about 15 months, and immunity has been shown to last anywhere from 12 to 18 months depending on the strain), so a yearly booster keeps that protection up to date. Annual re-vaccination is recommended for all at-risk dogs regardless of breed.
reference_contexts: As is typical for bacterin vaccines, annual boosters are required, with DOI shown for various vaccine serovars ranging from 12 to 18 mo.
Vaccines protect for at least 12 months, 141-143 with several manufacturers providing product guarantee for 15 months after proper administration.

Vaccines should be administered annually to all dogs starting at 12 weeks of age, regardless of breed, because leptospirosis is a zoonotic disease, can be severe or fatal despite treatment, and exposure can occur regardless of age, geography, or lifestyle.
review_note: Both gold sources agree: leptospirosis boosters are annual (once per year), unlike the 3-year interval for core vaccines. Reviewer should verify the numeric claims: minimum 12-month duration of immunity, ~15-month manufacturer guarantee (ACVIM), and the 12-to-18-month DOI range across serovars (AAHA). Note that leptospirosis is a noncore/lifestyle vaccine, so "need" presumes the dog is on the lepto vaccine and is at risk; both sources nonetheless recommend it for most/all dogs. Answer omits the puppy primary series (2 doses 4 weeks apart starting at/after 12 weeks) since the query asks specifically about adult boosters.
original_query: When does an adult dog need a leptospirosis booster?

user_input: What vaccines does my puppy need, and at what ages?
reference: A puppy's core vaccines protect against distemper, parvovirus, and adenovirus, and are usually given together in a single combination shot. The first dose is given at 6 to 8 weeks of age, then repeated every 2 to 4 weeks until the puppy is older than 16 weeks (a final dose around 18 to 20 weeks may be preferred in higher-risk areas). After this initial puppy series, one booster is given within a year, and after that boosters are needed only every 3 years rather than every year.
reference_contexts: CDV vaccines are considered core vaccines, recommended for all dogs regardless of geographical location... The minimum age to begin the primary vaccination protocol in puppies is 6-8 wk... Revaccination is therefore recommended at 2 to 4 wk intervals until greater than 16 wk old; 18-20 wk of age may be preferred particularly in areas of high CDV risk. After the primary puppy series of vaccinations, a booster should be administered within 1 yr. Thereafter, interval boosters every 3 yr are recommended; annual boosters are not necessary.

CPV MLV vaccines are considered core vaccines, recommended for all dogs regardless of geographical location... The minimum age to begin the primary vaccination protocol in puppies is 6-8 wk... Revaccination is therefore recommended at 2 to 4 wk intervals until greater than 16 wk old; 18-20 wk old is preferred particularly in areas of high CPV risk.

Current recommendations suggest that puppies should have the first (or primary) vaccination scheduled between the first 6 and 8 weeks of age, followed by several boosts administered in intervals of 3 or 4 weeks until 16 weeks of age... In adult dogs, vaccination should be carried out every 3 years.
review_note: Both gold sources directly and consistently answer the query. Reviewer should note a minor interval wording difference: AAHA states boosters "every 2 to 4 wk" until >16 wk, while the second source says "intervals of 3 or 4 weeks until 16 weeks" - I used AAHA's "2 to 4 weeks" and ">16 weeks" as the authoritative guideline figures. AAHA also classifies rabies as a core canine vaccine, but its timing is set by local law/jurisdiction rather than the numeric DAPP series schedule, so it is intentionally left out of the puppy-series numbers here. Verify the specific week numbers (6-8, 2-4 wk interval, >16, 18-20, 1 yr, every 3 yr) if precision is graded.
original_query: What is the recommended core vaccination schedule for puppies?

user_input: How do I keep my dog's teeth clean and healthy at home?
reference: Dental plaque and the bacteria in it play a key role in causing gum (periodontal) disease, and daily tooth brushing is considered the gold standard for preventing that disease from developing and getting worse. For brushing to be possible, you need to be able to handle your dog's mouth, which takes some skill, so it helps to train both yourself and your dog to accept a dental home-care routine early on. Keep an eye out for gums that bleed when you brush, since that is a sign of gum inflammation (gingivitis), and dogs whose teeth are brushed less often are more likely to have this bleeding.
reference_contexts: Daily tooth brushing is considered the gold standard for prevention of periodontal disease development and progression

Additionally, dental home care is not possible without the dog owner being able to handle the dog's mouth, which requires a certain amount of skill and training of both dog and owner. ... highlighting the need for early training of both dogs and owners in dental home care routines.

Gingival bleeding is an indication of gingivitis in both humans and in dogs. More than one third of dog owners reported oral bleeding when brushing ... brushing less frequently is associated with increased risk of bleeding
review_note: Only one of the two gold sources actually addresses at-home care: frontiers-fvets-2020-00298 supplies the daily-brushing-as-gold-standard fact, the need to train dog and owner to handle the mouth, and the gum-bleeding/gingivitis link. bmc-s12917-023-03668-3 is a study on qPCR/machine-learning DIAGNOSTIC tools for periodontitis and contributes only the background that dental plaque microbes drive periodontal disease; it has no home-care or prevention guidance. Marked partially_grounded because the corpus's home-care advice is limited to daily brushing plus mouth-handling training. Neither source covers other common home measures (dental chews, dental diets, specific toothpaste/oral rinses, or brushing frequency other than 'daily is best'), so the answer intentionally omits them. No dosages or numeric claims are stated in the reference; the '>1/3 owners reported bleeding' figure is study-population data and was not asserted as a general fact.
original_query: How can I take care of my dog's teeth and prevent dental disease at home?

user_input: My senior dog has ongoing pain, what are my options to manage it?
reference: Chronic pain in dogs is best managed with a multimodal approach that combines medications with non-drug therapies rather than relying on any single treatment. The main pain medications are anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), including newer options such as grapiprant (Galliprant), and these can be paired with drugs like amantadine or gabapentin; long-term use of oral opioids is not recommended for chronic pain. Just as important are non-drug measures: keeping your dog lean through weight management, omega-3 fatty acid supplements, and regular exercise and rehabilitation therapy such as daily walking or hydrotherapy. Additional supportive options include home changes like secure footing, ramps or steps, cold therapy, and, as an add-on, acupuncture.
reference_contexts: The guiding principles for the effective management of chronic pain are as follows: ... Use of a multimodal (combination therapy) approach. Chronic pain involves multiple and often complex changes in the sensory system. A combination of effective, known analgesics and nondrug therapies, combined with appropriate adjunctive therapies, is optimal.

Long-term use of oral opioids is not recommended for chronic pain control... There are several NSAIDs approved for use for chronic pain in dogs... Since 2016, grapiprant (Galliprant) has been approved in the United States for managing chronic pain in dogs... Amantadine ... was shown to be useful in combination with NSAIDs for the treatment of chronic OA pain

Although pharmacological agents are often necessary to assist with managing discomfort, nonpharmacological modalities are critically important in the management of chronic pain and maintaining the body in an active state... [maintenance of a lean body condition] for decreasing the rate of OA progression... the strength of evidence was low for all nutraceuticals except for omega-3 fatty acid in dogs... daily walking has been associated with a decrease in the severity of lameness in dogs with hip dysplasia... therapeutic exercises including hydrotherapy.
review_note: Fully grounded in the AAHA guideline, which has dedicated dog-specific sections on pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic chronic-pain management plus a tiered decision tree. Reviewer should verify drug specifics: grapiprant/Galliprant is named as US-approved for chronic pain in dogs (source ties it to 2016); the source notes gabapentin is widely used but has virtually no efficacy data for chronic pain in dogs, and lists amantadine only in combination with NSAIDs. I omitted anti-NGF monoclonal antibody (a tier-1 option in the dog decision tree) because the source states US approval was for cats; confirm if it should be included. No dosages are given in the reference.
original_query: What are the options for managing chronic pain in dogs?

user_input: How can I tell if my dog is in pain?
reference: The clearest way to tell if your dog is in pain is to watch for changes from their normal behavior, since deviations from what is normal for your dog suggest pain. Common signs include loss of appetite, being unusually quiet or calm, and changes in posture, in the way they walk or sit, in their overall demeanor, and in their ability to do everyday activities like climbing stairs. A dog with painful joints may hold a limb in an awkward position when resting or shift their weight off a sore leg, while a "tucked up" posture can point to belly pain and a straining posture can point to urinary or digestive discomfort. Pain is not always shown by crying out, so also look for subtler reactions like holding the breath, licking the lips, or looking away.
reference_contexts: In the clinic, pain assessment includes appetite, observation of demeanor, behavior, and palpation. Dogs adjust their demeanor, behavior, posture, and movement to minimize pain. Inappetence and calm behavior can represent subtle signs of pain... Owners know their dogs' normal behavior. Deviations from that behavior suggest the presence of pain.

At rest, awkward limb positions may indicate the presence of joint pain... When standing and moving, dogs shift weight away from a painful limb, and such postural abnormalities can be observed... A “tucked up” appearance can be an indicator of abdominal pain, and postural straining can be an indicator of lower urinary tract or lower gastrointestinal tract pain.
it can be necessary to educate the client on nonverbal or less severe reactions given by the patient (e.g., holding breath, licking of the lips, looking away) versus vocalization.
review_note: Source directly answers the query for dogs; all signs in the reference are drawn from dog-specific passages (the PDF also covers cats, which were excluded). "Changes in posture, gait, demeanor, and ability to perform daily activities" and "how is your dog climbing stairs" come from the owner-engagement and dog-assessment sections; the source frames these as what owners can watch for at home. No dosages or numbers involved. One caveat for the reviewer: the source presents the limb-position/weight-shift/"tucked up"/straining cues primarily as clinician observations, though it explicitly states owners can and should watch for the same behavioral changes at home.
original_query: How do I tell if my dog is in pain and what signs should I look for?

user_input: How do I keep my dog comfortable after surgery?
reference: After surgery, dogs are usually kept comfortable with a combination of pain medicines rather than a single drug. A typical plan for any surgery uses opioids, an anti-inflammatory (NSAID), and local anesthetics, together with cold packs and good nursing care. Local anesthetics are considered the most effective option and are recommended for every surgery; one long-acting form injected into the surgical wound at the end of the operation can numb the area for up to three days. Combining several of these approaches (a multimodal plan) generally controls pain better, reduces the need for extra opioid doses, and improves recovery, though anti-inflammatories are not the right choice for every dog.
reference_contexts: An appropriate starting point for every surgery is to plan on using opioids, an NSAID, and local anesthetics, in addition to cold therapy and appropriate nursing care. Local anesthetics are the most effective analgesic available in small animal practice, and they should be used in every surgery. ... NSAIDs may not be appropriate for every patient, and consideration needs to be given to whether they are provided prior to or after surgery. Opioids are very effective for perioperative pain and have proven preemptive benefit. Cold therapy is very effective and can be applied by owners.

The recently available long-acting preparation of bupivacaine is a liposome-encapsulated formulation, Nocita. When injected into the wound at the end of surgery, this agent can provide local analgesia that lasts up to 3 days.

although a multimodal approach, combining different analgesic strategies, may minimise side effects and improve postoperative recovery ... Multimodal analgesic protocols are crucial for effective pain management in dog mastectomy surgeries, minimising the need for rescue opioids.
review_note: Both gold sources directly answer the query. AAHA gives the owner-facing perioperative plan (opioids + NSAID + local anesthetics + cold therapy + nursing care); the mastectomy review confirms the same drug classes and the multimodal, opioid-sparing framing. Reviewer should verify: (1) the "up to 3 days" long-acting local anesthetic (Nocita/liposomal bupivacaine) is labeled by AAHA specifically for orthopedic surgery in dogs, so the 3-day figure is product/procedure-specific, not universal to all surgeries; (2) I deliberately omitted specific drug names and dosages (meloxicam, robenacoxib, methadone, fentanyl, tramadol, etc.) to keep the owner answer non-clinical and because the mastectomy dosing data is specific to mastectomy studies. No breed specifics involved.
original_query: What pain relief is appropriate for a dog after surgery?

user_input: My dog is overweight, how do I help him lose weight safely?
reference: Help your dog lose weight through a combination of controlled calorie reduction, the right food, and exercise, keeping the loss gradual: for dogs a safe pace is about 1 to 2 percent of body weight per week, because losing weight too fast leads to loss of muscle. Base how much you feed on your dog's ideal weight rather than its current weight, and keep treats and any other extra food items to no more than 10 percent of the day's total calories so the main diet still provides balanced nutrients. Combining reduced calories with exercise offers the best chance of lasting weight loss and helps preserve lean muscle, and a higher-protein, purpose-made weight-loss diet is preferred over simply feeding less of a regular food because it keeps nutrient intake adequate and helps protect muscle during calorie restriction. Weigh your dog and reassess regularly, since the starting calorie amount is only a starting point that needs adjusting over time.
reference_contexts: An effective individualized weight loss program provides a consistent and healthy rate of weight loss to reduce risk of disease, prevent malnutrition, and improve quality of life. Weight loss is achieved with appropriate caloric restriction, diet selection, exercise, and strategies to help modify the behavior of both the pet and client.
The desired rate of weight loss in dogs is 1–2%/wk, and in cats is 0.5–2%/wk. ... the patient is losing weight too rapidly (resulting in loss of muscle mass).

Incorporate a treat allowance of up to 10% of total calories into the daily caloric goal. ... Using a therapeutic weight-loss diet is preferred over using reduced amounts of over-the-counter (OTC) diets because therapeutic diets are more likely to provide adequate nutrient intake when fed in calorically restricted amounts. ... High protein may preserve muscle mass during weight loss ... Research in humans has shown that combining caloric reduction with exercise offers the best chance of successful and sustainable weight loss.
review_note: Both gold sources directly cover safe canine weight loss and corroborate each other. Reviewer should verify the load-bearing numbers: the 1–2%/week rate is dog-specific (cats are 0.5–2%/week), and the 10% cap applies to treats/extra food items relative to total daily calories. Feeding amounts are calculated from ideal body weight (e.g., 80% of ideal-weight RER); I kept this in lay terms rather than reproducing the RER equations. Both AAHA docs are dog-and-cat guidelines, so I scoped the answer to dogs as the query asks.
original_query: How do I help my overweight dog lose weight safely?

user_input: How do I choose a healthy food for my dog?
reference: Aim to feed your dog a complete and balanced diet in an amount that keeps them at a healthy weight. Check the food's AAFCO nutritional adequacy statement, which tells you whether a commercial diet contains all the required nutrients in the correct ratios for long-term feeding at a specific life stage; foods labeled "intermittent or supplemental" (including many therapeutic diets) do not meet that complete-and-balanced standard, while treats, snacks, and supplements are not required to carry the statement at all. Because energy and nutrient needs change across life stages such as growth and advancing age, match the food to your dog's current life stage. Keep that complete and balanced food as the main part of the diet (about 90% or more of total intake), with treats and other extras making up roughly 10% or less.
reference_contexts: When a cat or dog is healthy and maintains an appropriate weight, ensure the pet is being fed a complete and balanced diet in a suitable amount to avoid future unintended consequences.

The Association of American Feed Control Officials (AAFCO) nutritional adequacy statement indicates whether a commercial diet contains all the required nutrients in the correct ratios (i.e., “complete and balanced”) for long-term feeding to the specified life stage. Some foods, including many therapeutic diets, have an “intermittent or supplemental” use label indicating they do not meet the requirements of being “complete and balanced”... Treats, snacks, and supplements do not require a nutritional adequacy statement.

Ensure the calories consumed are within a reasonable level of agreement to MER and that the main source of complete and balanced nutrition represents ≥90% of total intake whereas treats and other food items make up ≤10%. Vulnerable life stages such as growth, gestation, lactation, and advancing age alter the patient’s energy and nutrient requirements.
review_note: Grounded in the AAHA 2021 nutrition/weight-management guideline, which covers both dogs and cats; I framed it to dogs. Verify the 90%/10% split (source states complete-and-balanced food should be >=90% of intake, treats/extras <=10%) and the life-stage list (growth, gestation, lactation, advancing age). "AAFCO" is a US labeling body; the statement specifics are US-market. No dosages or breed specifics involved.
original_query: What should I consider when choosing nutrition for my dog?

user_input: I have an Australian Shepherd, is the MDR1 gene mutation something I should worry about?
reference: Yes. The MDR1 mutation (also called the ABCB1-1Delta variant) is one of the most common in Australian Shepherds, which are consistently among the breeds with the highest rates of it. In one large genetic-testing group, about 32% of Australian Shepherds tested carried the mutation, and another study found this breed had the highest frequency of any it examined, at roughly 31%, with about 9% of dogs carrying two copies. Reported rates for Australian Shepherds are similar across Israel, the US, Europe and Japan (around 25 to 33%) and even higher in the UK and Australia (about 45%). The mutation is found in both standard and miniature Australian Shepherds.
reference_contexts: Among the relatively abundant breeds (sample size greater than 10 dogs, not including 37.5% for Old English Sheepdog where the sample size was only 4 dogs), it was highest for Australian Shepherds (31.4%, where 9.0% of 145 dogs were homozygotes for the mutation)

The frequencies observed for Australian Shepherd dogs living in Israel, US, Europe and Japan are similar, ranging from 25% to 33%, while higher frequencies were observed in the UK and Australia (~45%).

high variant allele frequencies are mainly seen in the collie, (miniature) Australian shepherd, Shetland sheepdog, and longhaired whippet ... Among the collie, Australian shepherd, Shetland sheepdog, and white Swiss shepherd breed, both del/del and wt/del dogs were found (del% of 58%, 32%, 31%, and 22%, respectively).
review_note: Reviewer verify the numbers, which come from specific study populations rather than universal rates and mix two related metrics. The ~32% is the "del%" (proportion of tested dogs carrying at least one copy, n=120) from the Belgian ABCB1 genetic-test cohort. The ~31.4% is an allele frequency (a different measure, not the same as percent of dogs) from an Israeli cohort, where 9.0% of 145 dogs were homozygous. The ~45% for the UK/Australia is also an allele frequency. Both sources use MDR1 and ABCB1-1Delta interchangeably. Answer correctly conveys "common / among the highest" for the breed, which both sources support directly.

user_input: My dog has the MDR1/ABCB1 mutation, which medications are dangerous?
reference: Dogs with the MDR1/ABCB1 mutation can have dangerous reactions to several common medications, because they lack the protein that normally keeps these drugs out of the brain, so the drugs build up and become toxic at doses that are safe for other dogs. The best-known risk is ivermectin and related parasite/deworming drugs (the macrocyclic lactones, such as doramectin, moxidectin, and milbemycin oxime), which can cause neurological signs like loss of coordination, lethargy, tremors, seizures, dilated pupils, blindness, coma, and even death. Other reported problem drugs include the anti-diarrhea medication loperamide, the sedative acepromazine, the opioid butorphanol, cyclosporine, and certain chemotherapy drugs such as vincristine, vinblastine, and doxorubicin, which can also damage the blood and bone marrow. Dogs carrying two copies of the mutation are affected most severely, but dogs with a single copy can also react to some of these drugs, particularly at higher doses.
reference_contexts: Dogs homozygous for the ABCB1-1Δ variant and thus without functional P-glycoproteins exhibit neurotoxic symptoms such as ataxia, lethargy, coma, tremors, seizures, mydriasis, and blindness at ivermectin doses that are not toxic for wildtype dogs. Ivermectin sensitivity was later renamed multidrug sensitivity since more drugs have been identified to cause neurotoxic symptoms or other adverse reactions in ABCB1-1Δ homozygous animals over the years, like various macrocyclic lactones [5], loperamide [6], acepromazine [7], and several chemotherapeutic agents [8].

Pertinent macrocyclic lactones include ivermectin, doramectin, moxidectin and milbemycin oxime. Other drugs commonly used in the veterinary clinic, such as P-glycoprotein substrates of the non-macrocyclic lactones type, were also reported as toxic to nt230(del4) MDR1 mutation homozygote dogs (−/−). These include vincristine, digoxin, mexiletine, quinidine, fexofenadine, vinblastine, and loperamide, cyclosporine A, verapamil, paclitexal, doxorubicin, dexamethasone and others

the recommended dosage for several treatments, such as treatment of generalized demodicosis with ivermectin [5], antidiarrheal treatment with loperamide [6], sedation with acepromazine [7], and lymphoma treatment with vincristine, vinblastine, or doxorubicin [8] were all shown to cause toxicity in multidrug sensitive dogs.
review_note: Both gold sources directly answer the query with overlapping drug lists. Reviewer should verify the drug names given (ivermectin, doramectin, moxidectin, milbemycin oxime, loperamide, acepromazine, butorphanol, cyclosporine, vincristine, vinblastine, doxorubicin) are all present in the source text — they are. I intentionally omitted the more obscure/less owner-relevant P-gp substrates listed in source 2 (digoxin, mexiletine, quinidine, fexofenadine, verapamil, paclitaxel, dexamethasone, apomorphine) to keep the answer readable for a dog owner; these are still valid source facts if a fuller list is wanted. Butorphanol and loperamide are described as opioid/P-gp substrates in source 2; acepromazine framed as a sedative per source 1. No specific numeric doses were included, so no dosage figures need checking beyond the qualitative "higher doses" statement, which is supported.
original_query: Which medications are dangerous for dogs with the MDR1 / ABCB1 mutation?

user_input: My dog has been vomiting and has diarrhea, what could be causing it?
reference: Sudden vomiting and diarrhea in dogs can have more than one cause. One is a disturbance in the normal balance of gut bacteria, which shows up in conditions like acute hemorrhagic diarrhea syndrome (also called hemorrhagic gastroenteritis) and in infections such as parvovirus or certain Clostridium bacteria. Heart problems can also contribute: as mitral valve disease or heart failure advances, reduced blood flow to the intestines and a weakened gut lining let bacteria and inflammation affect the gut, which can produce signs like diarrhea, vomiting, and reduced appetite. Diarrhea has been reported in up to 14 percent of dogs with congestive heart failure.
reference_contexts: In acute uncomplicated diarrhea (AD), dogs will develop a strong dysbiosis with a decrease in short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing bacteria... Similar alterations have been detected in dogs with acute hemorrhagic diarrhea syndrome (AHDS), also known as hemorrhagic gastroenteritis (HGE). ... Studies have shown an association between Clostridium perfringens and AHDS. ... The development of chronic enteropathies (CE) has been documented in dogs following episodes of parvovirus infection

Although there are no published studies specifically designed to assess GI signs in dogs with CVD, diarrhea has been reported in up to 14% dogs with CHF. ... Chronic CVD results in decreased GI mucosal perfusion due to physiologic shunting of blood away from the splanchnic circulation, leading to GI ischemia. ... This study indicates that dogs with MMVD have evidence of loss of gastrointestinal barrier function as evidenced by bacterial translocation as the disease progresses in severity, which may be associated with systemic inflammation.
Within the MMVD group, 8 dogs (all within Group 2) had a reported decrease in appetite... Diarrhea was reported in 3 dogs... One MMVD dog (Group 2) reported a history of vomiting once per week.
review_note: Gap probe: neither gold source is a general differential-diagnosis guide for acute vomiting + diarrhea. The corpus supports only a partial answer, covering (a) infectious/dysbiosis-related causes of acute diarrhea (hemorrhagic gastroenteritis/AHDS, C. perfringens, parvovirus, C. difficile) from fvets-2019-00498, and (b) heart disease (advanced MMVD / congestive heart failure) as a driver of GI signs including vomiting and diarrhea from mmvd-gi-translocation-plos-2025. It does NOT cover common acute causes an owner would expect (dietary indiscretion, toxins/poisons, foreign body, parasites as primary, pancreatitis). Note also fvets-2019-00498 discusses diarrhea specifically and does not address vomiting; the vomiting/appetite/diarrhea combination comes only from the heart-disease paper, where vomiting was reported in just 1 dog. Reviewer should verify the 14% CHF diarrhea figure (mmvd source, Introduction) and confirm whether an owner-facing answer this narrow is acceptable, or whether the graded answer should acknowledge the corpus does not comprehensively cover causes of acute vomiting and diarrhea. reference_contexts lightly normalize OCR spacing artifacts from the PDF text.

user_input: My dog had a seizure, how do vets diagnose epilepsy?
reference: Diagnosing epilepsy involves two steps: first confirming that your dog's episodes are truly epileptic seizures rather than another kind of event, then searching for an underlying cause. Because the most common form, idiopathic epilepsy, is a diagnosis of exclusion, a detailed history is the foundation, and the basic criteria are a history of two or more unprovoked seizures at least 24 hours apart, a first seizure between about six months and six years of age, a normal physical and neurological exam between seizures, and no significant abnormalities on routine blood tests and urinalysis. For a more confident diagnosis, a vet may add fasting and post-meal bile acid blood tests, an MRI of the brain, and analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid (the fluid around the brain and spinal cord). This fuller workup is especially recommended when seizures begin before six months or after six years of age, the neurological exam is abnormal, seizures come in clusters or as prolonged status epilepticus, or medication is not controlling them.
reference_contexts: The diagnostic approach to the patient presenting with a history of suspected epileptic seizures incorporates two fundamental steps: to establish if the events the animal is demonstrating truly represent epileptic seizures and if so, to identify their underlying cause.

Tier I confidence level for the diagnosis of IE is based on a history of two or more unprovoked epileptic seizures occurring at least 24 h apart, age at epileptic seizure onset of between six months and six years, unremarkable inter-ictal physical and neurological examination, and no significant abnormalities on minimum data base blood tests and urinalysis. Tier II confidence level for the diagnosis of IE is based on the factors listed in tier I and unremarkable fasting and post-prandial bile acids, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain (based on an epilepsy-specific brain MRI protocol) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis.

The authors recommend performing MRI of the brain and routine CSF analysis, after exclusion of reactive seizures, in dogs with age at epileptic seizure onset <6 months or >6 years, inter-ictal neurological abnormalities consistent with intracranial neurolocalisation, status epilepticus or cluster seizure at epileptic seizure onset, or a previous presumptive diagnosis of IE and drug-resistance with a single antiepileptic drug titrated to the highest tolerable dose.
review_note: Numbers to verify against source: seizures at least 24 h apart, onset window 6 months to 6 years, and the MRI/CSF triggers (onset <6mo or >6yr, abnormal neuro exam, cluster/status epilepticus, drug resistance) are quoted verbatim from the IVETF diagnostic-approach paper's abstract and Tier I/II criteria. The primary content comes from source #1 (neuro-ivetf-diagnostic-approach-epilepsy-dogs); source #2 (breed-aussie-epilepsy-ivetf-review) corroborates that idiopathic epilepsy is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring an appropriate diagnostic workup but is breed-review focused and adds no distinct diagnostic steps. Answer intentionally simplifies the paper's three-tier confidence system into the basic vs fuller workup rather than naming tiers.
original_query: How is epilepsy diagnosed in dogs?

user_input: My dog is getting older, what special care does a senior dog need?
reference: A senior dog needs a healthcare plan tailored to an aging body, which usually means a medical checkup once or twice a year (often with bloodwork and a urine test) so problems like kidney, liver, heart, or joint disease can be caught early. Good senior care covers many areas at once: managing pain and the reduced mobility that comes with arthritis, keeping up with dental care, adjusting nutrition (older dogs generally need fewer calories and more fiber, sometimes with a mild increase in protein to help preserve muscle), watching for signs of cognitive decline, and adapting the home environment. Because aging dogs are more prone to pain and distress, keeping them comfortable and protecting their quality of life is a central goal. Senior care also includes planning ahead for the eventual end-of-life stage, where the focus shifts to relieving suffering and supporting comfort.
reference_contexts: The senior dog or cat requires a tailored healthcare plan including preventive, diagnostic, and treatment protocols that are specific to the aging animal's physiologic needs... Optimal care of the senior pet involves a multifaceted approach, including diagnostics, medical and interventional therapies, pain management, nutrition, dentistry, anesthesia, modifying the environmental setting, managing behavioral problems, and recognizing and managing comorbidities. Senior care also includes educating and planning for end-of-life care for the patient

A medical workup is also recommended for senior pets once or twice a year and may include a complete blood count, chemistry, and urinalysis... A senior pet appointment may address issues such as decreased mobility from osteoarthritis, metabolic issues such as kidney or liver disease, and functional issues such as heart disease or neoplasia... pain and distress may be more common for senior animals. Mobility may be reduced owing to arthritic changes
senior dogs have decreased MER and need less caloric density and more fiber to optimize BCS. A senior diet may include mild increases in protein content and quality to compensate for LBM loss.
review_note: Primary grounding is aaha-senior-care-2023, which directly and comprehensively answers the query (tailored plan, 1-2x/year workup, mobility/pain, dental, nutrition, cognitive decline, environment, end-of-life planning). The 2016 end-of-life source is secondary: it supports framing end-of-life as a distinct life stage and the palliative goal of relieving suffering / protecting quality of life. Nutrition specifics translated from source jargon: MER = maintenance energy requirement (fewer calories), BCS = body condition score, LBM = lean body mass (muscle). Reviewer should verify the "once or twice a year" checkup frequency and the "fewer calories / more fiber / mild protein increase" nutrition summary, which are the most concrete claims.
original_query: What special care does a senior or geriatric dog need?

user_input: My dog collapsed and isn't breathing, how do I do CPR?
reference: If your dog is unresponsive and not breathing, start CPR right away: call for help, quickly clear any obvious blockage from the mouth or throat without delaying compressions by more than 10 to 15 seconds, and lay the dog on its side. Place your overlapping hands with the heels over the widest part of the chest (for round-chested dogs like retrievers or pit bull types) or directly over the heart (for narrow, keel-chested dogs like sighthounds), and push at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute, compressing about one-third to one-half of the width of the chest and letting the chest spring all the way back up between each push. Working alone, give 30 compressions followed by 2 breaths, delivered through a tight-fitting face mask or mouth-to-nose with the head and neck held in line with the spine, then immediately start another round of 30 compressions. Keep repeating these cycles until help arrives or the dog revives; if giving mouth-to-nose breaths would put you at risk, do compression-only CPR instead.
reference_contexts: Chest compressions are performed at 100–120/min in dogs and cats (BLS-07). In dogs and cats in lateral recumbency, we recommend providing chest compressions to a depth of one-third to one-half of the width of the thorax at the compression point (BLS-18)... The compressor must allow full recoil of the thorax between compressions to allow the heart to refill with blood (BLS-01).

In medium- to giant-sized, keel-chested dogs such as Sighthounds, we recommend the compressor's overlapping hands be placed with the heels directly over the dog's heart (BLS-03)... In medium- to giant-sized, round-chested dogs such as Retrievers and Pitbull-type dogs, we recommend the compressor's overlapping hands be placed with the heels over the widest portion of the thorax (BLS-02).

During single-rescuer BLS, we recommend a compression-to-ventilation (C:V) ratio of 30 compressions:2 breaths (30:2) (BLS-09). The rescuer delivers 30 chest compressions at the recommended rate, then, during a chest compression pause of no more than a few seconds, delivers 2 breaths, and immediately begins another round of 30 chest compressions... Nonintubated dogs and cats should be ventilated using a tight-fitting facemask... If no tight-fitting facemask is available, we recommend provision of rescue breaths by the mouth-to-nose technique unless there is risk to the rescuer... If the rescuer believes there is personal risk involved in providing mouth-to-nose rescue breaths, chest compression-only CPR should be performed (BLS-10).
review_note: Both RECOVER 2024 sources directly cover owner-performable CPR technique. Reviewer should verify the load-bearing numbers, all taken verbatim from the source: compression rate 100-120/min; depth one-third to one-half of chest width in lateral recumbency; single-rescuer ratio 30:2; airway check should not delay compressions by more than 10-15 seconds. Breed-specific hand placement is source-accurate (heart for keel-chested sighthounds; widest part of thorax for round-chested retrievers/pit bull types). The answer targets the common single-rescuer, dog-on-its-side (lateral recumbency) scenario; the source also covers dorsal recumbency (one-fourth of thoracic depth) and multi-rescuer/intubated cases, which were omitted as out of scope for an owner doing hands-on CPR. "Let the chest spring all the way back up" paraphrases "allow full recoil of the thorax."

user_input: How do I protect my dog from heartworm?
reference: The main recommendation is to give dogs an FDA-approved heartworm preventive medication year-round, not just during warm months. Alongside the medication, it helps to reduce mosquito exposure by controlling mosquitoes and their breeding areas, using an EPA-approved mosquito repellent product on the dog, and when possible keeping the dog out of the outdoors during peak mosquito feeding times. A veterinarian must prescribe the preventive, and dogs older than about 7 months (or without a heartworm test in the past 12 months) should be tested before starting a preventive product.
reference_contexts: AHS and the FDA recommend year-round administration of FDA-approved preventive drugs to prevent heartworm infection and enhance compliance/adherence.

Application of an EPA-approved mosquito repellent/ectoparasiticide has been shown to increase the overall efficacy of a heartworm prevention program by controlling the mosquito vector in laboratory studies... In addition, reduction of exposure to mosquitoes through standard environmental control of mosquitoes and their breeding environments, and when possible, reducing outdoor exposure during key mosquito feeding periods is recommended.

The prescription and subsequent administration of heartworm preventive medication requires authorization by a licensed veterinarian... In dogs >7 months of age and/or if records of testing within the past 12 months do not exist, it is necessary to test (antigen and microfilariae) the patient before dispensing or prescribing a preventive product

user_input: My dog is constantly itchy and scratching, could it be allergies, and how is it treated?
reference: Atopic dermatitis is diagnosed by matching a dog's history and itchy skin signs to clinical criteria while ruling out other conditions that look similar, using tools like flea combing, skin scrapings, and cytology; dogs with year-round itching or stomach and gut signs also need a strict elimination-diet trial, and once the diagnosis is confirmed, allergy testing can pinpoint the triggering allergens. Treatment is layered: sudden flare-ups are handled by finding and removing the trigger, bathing with mild shampoos, and easing the itch with topical or oral steroids or oclacitinib. For long-term (chronic) cases, the focus is avoiding flare triggers and keeping the skin and coat well cared for, including more frequent bathing and possibly added essential fatty acids, with the most effective itch-reducing medications being topical and oral steroids, oral ciclosporin, oral oclacitinib, and injectable interferons where available. Allergen-specific immunotherapy (allergy shots) and regular preventive use of topical steroids are the main ways to prevent or delay future flares, and plans are usually combined and tailored to the individual dog.
reference_contexts: The diagnosis of canine AD is based on meeting clinical criteria and ruling out other possible causes with similar clinical signs. Flea combing, skin scraping and cytology should be performed, where necessary, as part of a thorough work-up. Elimination diet trials are required for patients with perennial pruritus and/or concurrent gastrointestinal signs. Once a clinical diagnosis of canine AD is made, allergy testing can be performed to identify potential causative allergens for allergen-specific immunotherapy.

The treatment of acute flares of AD should involve the search for, and then elimination of, the cause of the flares, bathing with mild shampoos, and controlling pruritus and skin lesions with interventions that include topical and/or oral glucocorticoids or oclacitinib. For chronic canine AD, the first steps in management are the identification and avoidance of flare factors, as well as ensuring that there is adequate skin and coat hygiene and care; this might include more frequent bathing and possibly increasing essential fatty acid intake. The medications currently most effective in reducing chronic pruritus and skin lesions are topical and oral glucocorticoids, oral ciclosporin, oral oclacitinib, and, where available, injectable recombinant interferons.
Allergen-specific immunotherapy and proactive intermittent topical glucocorticoid applications are the only interventions likely to prevent or delay the recurrence of flares of AD.
review_note: Both gold sources (diagnosis guidelines + ICADA 2015 treatment update) directly answer the query; the reference is drawn from their abstracts/conclusions. Reviewer should verify drug names, which are copied verbatim from the source: oclacitinib, ciclosporin, and injectable recombinant interferons. No dosages are stated in the source or the reference. Plain-language glosses added by me and worth a check: "glucocorticoids" rendered as "steroids", "pruritus" as "itch", "perennial" as "year-round", and "allergen-specific immunotherapy" as "allergy shots".
original_query: How is canine atopic dermatitis diagnosed and treated?

user_input: My dog was diagnosed with hip dysplasia, how is it managed?
reference: Hip dysplasia is usually managed conservatively first, which means controlling the dog's weight, limiting intense or painful exercise, using physical therapy, and giving pain relievers (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) or joint supplements to ease discomfort and keep the joint moving. Gentle, low-impact activity such as off-leash walking or swimming is recommended to build muscle strength and improve the joint's range of motion. Injections into the joint, such as hyaluronan, corticosteroids, or platelet-rich plasma, can also help control pain and inflammation. When the disease is severe and causes pain and disability, surgery becomes an option, ranging from joint-realignment procedures in young dogs to salvage surgeries like femoral head and neck removal or total hip replacement.
reference_contexts: Conservative treatment is often considered the first-line therapy at the onset of HD clinical signs, ensuring the relief of discomfort and pain, the preservation of limb function and range of motion... conservative treatment entails limiting intense and painful exercise, weight control, physical therapy, and administration of analgesics or nutraceuticals. Slight, low impact and high-resistance exercise, based on off-leash walking or swimming are recommended, as these exercises improve muscle mass strength and joint range of motion. In mature canines, it is centred on treating OA-related pain, by using non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
Furthermore, intra-articular administration of hyaluronan, corticosteroids, platelet-rich plasma, or ozone gas are also considered an alternative when controlling joint pain and inflammation.

Regarding non-conservative management, surgical alternatives for young animals are designed as a preventive measure, ensuring improved joint alignment... For dogs displaying symptomatic disability and pain with severe degenerative joint disease, joint capsular denervation, femoral head and neck ostectomy, and total hip replacement are the existing salvage surgical procedures.
review_note: Reference is grounded almost entirely in bmc-s12917-023-03777-z, which directly and completely covers conservative and surgical management of canine hip dysplasia. The second gold source (breed-aussie-hip-elbow-dysplasia-selection) is about population-level PREVENTION via genetic/breeding selection and radiographic screening, not clinical management of an affected dog; it only corroborates weight/nutrition/growth rate as environmental factors. If the grader intends "management" to include herd/breed-level prevention (screening + selective breeding to reduce prevalence), the answer could be extended with that angle from the aussie source. Reviewer should verify: specific surgical procedure names (femoral head and neck ostectomy, total hip replacement, juvenile pubic symphysiodesis, pelvic osteotomies) and that "nutraceuticals/joint supplements" phrasing is acceptable for owner-facing text. No dosages are stated in the source.

user_input: My dog seems really lethargic and won't eat, should I be worried?
reference: Low energy and eating less or refusing food are among the common signs that can point to an underlying illness in dogs, particularly as they get older. These changes often appear alongside other signs such as a generally unwell or "off" demeanor, behavior changes, drinking more or less than usual, gradual weight loss, and reduced mobility. Because these signs can have many causes, it is worth having your dog examined so that a physical check and tests like a blood profile and urine test can help find what is going on.
reference_contexts: Common clinical signs of chronic disease may include malaise, progressive lethargy, behavior changes, hyporexia, anorexia, altered thirst pattern, weight loss over time, mobility alterations, and nonhealing wounds.

A suspected chronic disease can often be presumptively diagnosed based on the client's account of the pet's history and physical examination, although it is recommended to perform appropriate clinicopathological evaluations. The minimum database for a senior pet should include a detailed blood profile including thyroid panel and urinalysis.

A thorough history can provide important information to assess the pet's health and may include exploring the patient's eating and drinking habits, exercise, movement, play behavior, eliminations, attitude, grooming, vision, and hearing.
review_note: Gap-probe as flagged. Only one of the two gold sources actually answers the query. aaha-senior-care-2023 supports the answer: it lists "progressive lethargy," "hyporexia" (reduced appetite) and "anorexia" (not eating) as common clinical signs of chronic disease, and recommends history + physical exam + blood profile/urinalysis to reach a diagnosis. Caveats for the reviewer: (1) this passage is scoped to SENIOR dogs and is clinician-facing, so the "particularly as they get older" framing is faithful to the source but the guideline does not speak to young/adult dogs; (2) the source gives NO acute-emergency threshold or "worry after X hours" guidance, so the reference deliberately does not quantify urgency. The second gold source, fvets-2019-00498 (canine gut microbiome/metabolome review), does NOT address lethargy or when-to-worry for owners; its only appetite mention is that a probiotic "increased the well-being of the dogs by maintaining appetite" - not relevant symptom guidance - so it was not used.
original_query: My dog seems lethargic and is not eating, should I be worried?
